summary: This experimental memo describes the architecture behind the Group Key Management Protocol: how grouped symmetric keys can be created and distributed among communicating peers. The detailed protocol is in the companion RFC 2093.

plainLanguage.summary: The Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP) architecture lets members of a multicast group create and distribute shared encryption keys without asking a central key server for each group operation. A group controller coordinates the work, while a separate security-management function assigns identities and permissions.

questions: how do groups share symmetric keys
how does group key management work
what is a group key controller
sender initiated vs receiver initiated multicast keys
subtitle: An architecture for creating and sharing symmetric keys among multicast group members.

tldr.problem: A multicast group needs a shared encryption key, but a central key-distribution site can add delay and become a bottleneck or single point of failure.
tldr.mechanism: GKMP delegates group-key creation, distribution, and rekeying to a designated group controller and the communicating members, with network-wide permissions still managed separately.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents an Experimental architecture and leaves issues such as access-control policy and recovery from lost messages for further work.

today: RFC 2094 is Experimental. Its text describes an architecture and lists unresolved issues rather than specifying an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Manage Group Keys Without a Central Server
sections.content:
Multicast sends common information to a group, so members need a shared symmetric key when the data must be confidential. Traditional arrangements use a key distribution center to approve a group and deliver its key to each member.

The RFC proposes shifting routine group-key work to the communicating parties. It still assumes a security manager supplies authenticated identities and permission information; GKMP does not define how that authority is organized.
sections.plainLanguage: Group members need the same secret key to protect multicast data. GKMP moves the day-to-day key work to those members, but it still depends on a security manager to establish their permissions.

sections.title: Two Ways to Start a Group
sections.content:
In sender-initiated operation, the sender selects the group members and acts as the group-key controller. It creates a group key packet with a member, checks each member's permissions, and sends that member a protected package containing session keys and the group key information.

In receiver-initiated operation, a member contacts a controller to join. The controller may be selected by voting, a default rule, or configuration. In either model, one controller is active for the group at a time, and the controller distributes new group-key material when rekeying is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can choose the group and control its key, or receivers can contact a selected controller to join. The controller checks permissions and delivers the key material to members.

sections.title: Roles and Supporting Functions
sections.content:
The group controller creates keys, sends key-distribution messages, initiates rekeying, and reports progress. A receiver checks that the controller is authorized, accepts or requests key material, maintains local certificate-revocation information, and manages its local keys.

Group management supplies the membership list and network-related information. Security management handles host identity, permission certificates, software initialization, and compromise recovery. The RFC keeps those supporting functions distinct from GKMP's cryptographic key tasks.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller manages the group's keys; other members check and receive them. Separate management functions provide the member list and decide which hosts have permission to participate.

sections.title: Establishment, Rekeying, and Removal
sections.content:
To establish a group, a controller checks the create-group command, creates keys with a member, verifies each member's identity and permissions, and distributes the keys. During rekeying, the controller creates new keys and sends them to the group protected with key material already shared by members.

Removing a trusted member can use a command and acknowledgment. Removing a compromised member requires creating a new group without that member. The RFC describes a security-versus-continuity choice and does not mandate one policy for every network.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller checks members before distributing keys and later sends replacement keys to the group. If a member is compromised, the group can be rebuilt without that member, but the RFC leaves the timing decision to the network.

sections.title: Open Issues and Experimental Status
sections.content:
The RFC identifies unresolved questions about access control, operation across security levels, and handling delayed, lost, or maliciously disrupted messages. It notes that multicast delivery may not reach every member and that the group needs recovery procedures.

GKMP distributes work and avoids consulting a central key site for each routine action, but permissions still come from network-wide security management. The document is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The design still leaves important policy and message-recovery questions open. It is an Experimental architecture, not a finished Internet standard.
